newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bass posts 10 pct profit rise, shares drop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bass posts 10 pct profit rise, shares drop.

text.p: British brewing-to-hotels group Bass Plc posted a ten percent rise in profits on Wednesday, driven by a buoyant performance in its managed pubs and 2,200-strong Holiday Inn hotels empire.

Yet its shares dropped sharply after chairman Sir Ian Prosser adopted a cautious stance on the group's outlook and amid concern about the possibility of slower growth on the hotels side, analysts said.

There was continuing concern too about Bass's planned acquisition of the Carlsberg-Tetley brewing group, seen as important in boosting its UK activities but which is yet to be cleared by the recently-elected Labour government.
Bass dropped 24-1/2p or three percent to 796-1/2, among the biggest decliners in the FTSE 100 index.

The group reported a 10 percent increase in profits before tax to 318 million pounds ($526.2 million) in the six months to April 12. Forecasts had mostly ranged from 305 million pounds to 325 million.

"The results were pretty much in line with expectations, but it was indicated at the meeting that there was an oversupply of economy hotels where most of the group's growth is currently coming from," said Colin Davies, analyst at Goldman Sachs.
There were also worries among analysts about the long wait for a government decision on the group's Carlsberg-Tetley acquisition.
The company first announced its plan to acquire the brewer in August but said on Wednesday it did not expect a decision on whether the deal could go ahead until mid-June.
"The company told us it is not expecting to hear before mid-June on Carlsberg-Tetley and obviously the market wants to hear as soon as possible," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
"They were also perhaps not as upbeat on the outlook as on previous occasions," he added.
However Chairman Sir Ian Prosser said conditions in Germany and France had reached their low point and were now on their way back up.

"Germany and France have probably bottomed out and are now on the way back up, and in America we are continuing to see good economic growth. We are seeing most central banks taking action against inflation," Prosser told Reuters.

Bass hopes the new British Labour government will reach a decision on the group's proposed acquisition of Carlsberg-Tetley in the middle of next month. "I would guess mid-June we might hear," said Prosser.
Labour is widely expected to impose more stringent conditions on the merger than the former Conservative government or even block it altogether.
The merger would create Britain's largest brewer with a 35 percent share of the market. Uncertainty over the outcome of Bass's bid for C-T has continued to depress its share price.

Asked what other uncertainties a change of government brought for the group, Prosser said: "Their attitude over a minimum wage and where they would set that. I think it should be set at a relatively low figure and phased in over a period of time to give companies a chance to accommodate it."

Britain's largest trade union, UNISON, representing 1.3 million public sector workers, is asking the government to impose a minimum wage of 4.42 pounds an hour. Labour plans to set up a Low Pay Commission to take evidence from employers and unions before recommending a minimum wage.

The introduction of a minimum wage is likely to affect the food, drink and retail sector, especially given the high number of part time, low-paid staff employed. Bass employs about 70,000 people, including 50,000 in its British pubs, most of them as bar staff.
Bass said the profits rise was driven by its managed pubs and Holiday Inn hotels.

Prosser said the company should add a total 200 managed pubs by the year end, after adding in 83 in the first half. The group's pub outlets include Harvester restaurants, O'Neill's Irish bars and Vintage Inns.
Group capital expenditure will be reduced to 620 million pounds for the year as a whole from an original forecast of 750 million, said Prosser.
This was mainly because the acquisition of 60 Holiday Inns in North America by the Bristol Hotel Company means Bass no longer needs to spend on maintaining them.
The Bass-owned Gala chain of bingo halls, the one area of weakness in the group's half year results, was being looked at hard and management had been changed, said Prosser.
Gala's trading profit fell 6.0 million pounds to 13 million in the half year as competition intensified and more new clubs opened up.

Group turnover grew by 6.8 percent to 2.69 billion pounds. Holiday Inn's improved operating profit 5.3 percent to 80 million pounds, or 10.2 percent in dollar terms, as average room rates in America rose sharply.

Bass' 2,812 managed pubs raised trading profits by 12.6 percent to 116 million pounds while the group's leisure division, which includes Gala and Coral betting shops, raised profits by 11.4 percent to 39 million.

Profits from the beer business were 6.9 percent higher in the first half of 1997 than in 1996 at 77 million pounds, with key brands Carling Black Label and Worthington draught bitter performing strongly.
($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
